frase_gancho.texto: A jade ax that never cut anything: the face of a supernatural jaguar.

puente_narrativo.texto: From jade, the quintessential Olmec material, we move on to rubber, their other treasure. Look for a U-shaped stone belt with a toad on the front: it is an image of the ballgame.

guion_corto.texto: This jade ax, about twenty-eight centimeters tall, was not made to cut wood. It is a votive ax: an object of offering and of prestige. At the top it bears the face of a supernatural being that blends human and jaguar features: almond-shaped eyes, eyebrows like flames, and an open mouth with the corners turned down. Most distinctive is the V-shaped cleft at the top of the head, which is linked to the sprouting of maize. The body narrows toward the bottom, until it forms a symmetrical blade. The Olmec valued jade above any other material: it was the color of water, of young maize, of life. This type of ax is known as the “Kunz type.”

guion_largo.texto:
An ax that does not cut. It seems like a contradiction, but it is a clue: for the Olmec, what mattered about this object was not its blade, but its form and its material. It is an ax turned into an emblem and an offering. That is why it is called votive: it was offered to the gods, or displayed as a sign of rank. You have already seen six, set in a row, in [Offering 4](mna_s08_ofrenda4_laventa) from La Venta.

Jade is extremely hard and cannot be carved with metal: it is polished with sand, water and patience, over weeks. That is why a jade ax was a treasure: in each one there are weeks of work, as in the [rock crystal cup](mna_s07_copa_cristal_roca) from Oaxaca. And the jade, moreover, had to come from far away. It is thought that a good part of Olmec jade arrived from Guatemala, hundreds of kilometers away, along trade routes.

Look at the face, up top. It is not entirely human nor entirely animal. It has slanted eyes, as if half closed; eyebrows that look like flames; and an open mouth, with downturned corners, the mouth you already know from the Olmec babies. Specialists describe it as a supernatural being with jaguar features. Above the forehead, the head splits into a V-shaped cleft. It has been interpreted as the point where the maize plant sprouts from the god’s head, or as the cleft of a sacred mountain.

For the Olmec, the polished stone ax was the tool that opened the jungle for planting. That is why it became a symbol of agriculture and fertility. Some researchers also link it to lightning, which strikes the earth so that water may spring forth, the same idea that centuries later would be embodied by [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo). An ax, a lightning bolt and a maize sprout: three ideas in a single object.

What happened afterward with these axes is curious. Two thousand years later, the Mexica found Olmec objects, from a culture that was already very far back in time, and kept them, as relics, in the offerings of the Templo Mayor. Olmec pieces have been found buried there. That is, the Mexica already treated this culture as a venerable antiquity, just as you do now.

The name “Kunz type” comes from a similar, famous ax that the gemologist George F. Kunz bought in 1890, and which today is kept in New York, at the Museum of Natural History. It is another Mexican piece that lives far from home, like the Penacho de Viena. Specialists call those that resemble it “Kunz type”: an elegant, symmetrical form, with a figure at the top.

Think of the whole: an ax that does not cut, a jaguar that does not roar, a maize sprout that never grows. Everything in this piece is made to say something more than what can be seen. And perhaps that is the most lasting Olmec legacy: the idea that objects can be symbols as powerful as the jungle itself.

texto: Find the V-shaped cleft at the top of the head
Observe the eyebrows like flames and the open mouth
Notice how the ax narrows toward the bottom, until it forms a blade

texto.Dimensions: 0.29 m high x 0.135 m wide x 0.03 m thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Olmec jade axes were working tools.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were emblems and offerings. Jade was worth more as a symbol than as a tool, and these axes were not meant to cut.
